scenes.tts: Lifting a cup and lifting a suitcase can use the same muscle. Who decides how hard it pulls?
scenes.visual: Split screen: a hand lifting a coffee cup, then a hand lifting a full suitcase. The forearm muscle is outlined in both. The question appears: Who decides?
scenes.narration: Lifting a cup and lifting a suitcase can use the same muscle. Who decides how hard it pulls?

scenes.tts: The decision ends in the spinal cord, at cells called alpha motor neurons.
scenes.visual: A spinal cord cross-section draws in. A motor neuron in the ventral horn glows; its axon leaves through the ventral root. Label: alpha motor neuron.
scenes.narration: The decision ends in the spinal cord, at cells called alpha motor neurons.

scenes.tts: Each motor neuron's axon branches to many muscle fibres. The neuron and its fibres make one motor unit.
scenes.visual: The axon runs out to a muscle and branches to a scattered set of fibres. A bracket labels neuron plus fibres: motor unit.
scenes.narration: Each motor neuron's axon branches to many muscle fibres. The neuron and its fibres make one motor unit.

scenes.tts: One spike normally makes every fibre of its unit twitch.
scenes.visual: A single spike travels down the axon; every fibre of that unit lights at once and twitches. Other fibres stay dark.
scenes.narration: One spike normally makes every fibre of its unit twitch.

scenes.tts: All the motor neurons that supply one muscle make up its motor pool.
scenes.visual: Zoom out: a cluster of motor neurons of different sizes in the ventral horn, all projecting to the same muscle. Label: motor pool.
scenes.narration: All the motor neurons that supply one muscle make up its motor pool.

scenes.tts: Commands come from the brain, stretch sensors, pain and rhythm circuits.
scenes.visual: Arrows converge on one motor neuron from four sources, each labelled: brain, muscle spindle (stretch), skin pain receptor, rhythm circuit. The brain, pain and rhythm arrows pass through small interneurons first; only the spindle arrow lands directly.
scenes.narration: Commands come from the brain, stretch sensors, pain and rhythm circuits.

scenes.tts: All of them end on the motor neurons. Sherrington called them the final common path.
scenes.visual: The four arrows merge into the motor neuron. Label appears: the final common path (Sherrington).
scenes.narration: All of them end on the motor neurons. Sherrington called them the final common path.

scenes.tts: Picture one motor neuron's voltage as a bar, with a line at threshold.
scenes.visual: Beside the motor neuron, a vertical voltage bar with a dashed horizontal line marked threshold.
scenes.narration: Picture one motor neuron's voltage as a bar, with a line at threshold.

scenes.tts: Excitation pushes the bar up, toward the line. Inhibition holds it back.
scenes.visual: Two panels. Left: green arrows (excitation) push the bar up; red arrows (inhibition) pull it down, away from threshold. Right: the same excitatory push with inhibitory channels open gives a smaller rise (shunt). Both panels labelled: less likely to fire.
scenes.narration: Excitation pushes the bar up, toward the line. Inhibition holds it back.

scenes.tts: Usually it pulls the bar down. Its open channels also blunt excitation.
scenes.visual: Hold on the two panels: the downward pull on the left, the blunted rise on the right. Label: inhibition opens channels.
scenes.narration: Usually it pulls the bar down. Its open channels also blunt excitation.

scenes.tts: When the net current lifts the bar to the line, the cell fires.
scenes.visual: The bar crosses the threshold line; the cell flashes a spike and its unit's fibres twitch. Bar labelled: voltage change from rest. On screen: for steady or slowly rising input, net current x input resistance reaches threshold, so the cell fires.
scenes.narration: When the net current lifts the bar to the line, the cell fires.

scenes.tts: So ask two questions of any spinal circuit. Which motor pools does it push up, and which down?
scenes.visual: Card with the first question: Which motor pools does it push up, and which down?
scenes.narration: So ask two questions of any spinal circuit. Which motor pools does it push up, and which down?

scenes.tts: And within a pool, which cells reach threshold first?
scenes.visual: The second question joins the card: Within a pool, which cells reach threshold first?
scenes.narration: And within a pool, which cells reach threshold first?

scenes.tts: Take a pool of small cells, which make weak units, and large cells, which make strong units.
scenes.visual: Three motor neurons of different sizes, small, medium and large, each with a voltage bar and threshold line. Their units drawn beside: few fibres, more, many.
scenes.narration: Take a pool of small cells, which make weak units, and large cells, which make strong units.

scenes.tts: The input to the whole pool rises a little at a time. Which cells fire first?
scenes.visual: One shared input arrow feeds all three cells, with a dial labelled input turning slowly upward. Question on screen: Which fires first?
scenes.narration: The input to the whole pool rises a little at a time. Which cells fire first?

scenes.tts: The small ones. Many people guess the large ones, because big seems strong.
scenes.visual: The small cell's bar climbs fastest and crosses threshold first, then the medium, then the large. A crossed-out thought bubble: big = strong = first?
scenes.narration: The small ones. Many people guess the large ones, because big seems strong.

scenes.tts: Firing depends on how far the input moves the voltage. The same input moves a small cell further.
scenes.visual: The three bars side by side under equal input: the small cell's bar is highest. Label: same input, bigger voltage change in the small cell.
scenes.narration: Firing depends on how far the input moves the voltage. The same input moves a small cell further.

scenes.tts: A small cell has less membrane, so fewer ways for current to leave. Its input resistance is higher.
scenes.visual: Close-up of a small and a large cell membrane with open channels drawn as exits; the small cell has fewer. Label: higher input resistance, R_in.
scenes.narration: A small cell has less membrane, so fewer ways for current to leave. Its input resistance is higher.

scenes.tts: Think of a bathtub with fewer drains. The same inflow raises the water higher.
scenes.visual: Two bathtubs with the same tap flow: one with two drains, one with many. The water stands higher in the tub with fewer drains.
scenes.narration: Think of a bathtub with fewer drains. The same inflow raises the water higher.

scenes.tts: On screen is Ohm's law for a motor neuron. Higher input resistance means less current is needed.
scenes.visual: Formula box, not read aloud: ΔV = I × R_in, so I_th = ΔV_th / R_in (steady or slowly rising input; equal ΔV_th). Higher R_in, less current needed, recruited earlier.
scenes.narration: On screen is Ohm's law for a motor neuron. Higher input resistance means less current is needed.

scenes.tts: That order, small before large, is the size principle. Under shared input it is a strong tendency, not a law.
scenes.visual: Recruitment staircase: small, then medium, then large cross threshold in turn. Title: the size principle (Henneman, cats, 1957). Tag: a strong tendency, not a law.
scenes.narration: That order, small before large, is the size principle. Under shared input it is a strong tendency, not a law.

scenes.tts: There is a catch. A large cell has room for more synapses, so it can collect more input.
scenes.visual: The large cell sprouts extra synapse dots and collects more input arrows.
scenes.narration: There is a catch. A large cell has room for more synapses, so it can collect more input.

scenes.tts: In this simple model, small cells still go first if effective current grows less steeply with size than input resistance falls. Real current distributions depend on the pathway.
scenes.visual: Two lines on log scales against cell size, labelled hypothetical example: effective current I_eff ∝ A^α rises gently; input resistance R_in ∝ A^−β falls steeply. Labels: equal required voltage changes; condition α < β. Their product, the voltage change ΔV ∝ A^(α−β), still falls with size. Footnote: measured homonymous Ia effective currents in cat medial gastrocnemius were larger, on average, in the high-resistance cells.
scenes.narration: In this simple model, small cells still go first if effective current grows less steeply with size than input resistance falls. Real current distributions depend on the pathway.

scenes.tts: So, with equal thresholds, the small cells still go first.
scenes.visual: Back to the three voltage bars under the larger shared input: the small cell's bar still crosses first. Label: equal thresholds assumed.
scenes.narration: So, with equal thresholds, the small cells still go first.

scenes.tts: A pool has a second way to add force. Active units fire faster, so their twitches add up.
scenes.visual: Twitch train for one unit: spikes far apart give separate bumps; closer spikes make the bumps ride on each other and the force line climbs.
scenes.narration: A pool has a second way to add force. Active units fire faster, so their twitches add up.

scenes.tts: Every command ends as current on motor neurons. Which pools go up or down, and who fires first?
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: Every command ends as synaptic current on motor neurons. Which pools go up, which down? Within a pool, who reaches threshold first? Force grows by recruitment and by faster firing.
scenes.narration: Every command ends as current on motor neurons. Which pools go up or down, and who fires first?
